sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. ... Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... Ask them why this might be ... Listen to their response ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Check with the pediatrician first; a change like a new child-care routine is a common cause; ask the child why and listen; hugs, praise and stickers on a chart; it usually does not last very long, a few days or weeks in many cases. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up ... constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins
sources.supports: From about age 3 children can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticize or punish; say you know, that it is okay and that next time will go better; ask for help cleaning up; constant asking can make a child hold back until it is too late; avoid returning to diapers, use training pants, the potty in the child's room, going with the child to the preschool bathroom. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, date reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals ... Offer your child small rewards, such as stickers or time reading, every time your child goes in the potty. ... Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. ... It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. Reassure your child that he or she is well on the way to using the potty like a big kid.
sources.supports: Sit on the potty 15 to 30 minutes after meals, small rewards like stickers or reading time, praise every attempt even if nothing happens, no punishment and no disappointed face, say it was an accident and reassure the child. A Nemours page for parents.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy

post_text.fb_text:
פעם הייתי אלוף הסיר 🚽
חודשיים שלמים בלי פספוס.
הייתי רץ לשירותים לבד,
וכל פעם קיבלתי מדבקה על הלוח.
הרגשתי גדול, כמו הילדים בגן.

ידעתי לבד מתי צריך
הבטן שלי הייתה אומרת לי,
והייתי עוצר באמצע המשחק.
לא הייתם צריכים לשאול אותי.
זה היה שלי.

ואז עברנו לגן החדש
חדרים אחרים, שירותים גדולים,
וילדים שאני עוד לא מכיר.
פתאום הכול התבלבל,
גם הבטן שלי.

אני מחביא את המכנסיים
כשזה קורה, אני מתבייש.
אז אני דוחף אותם מאחורי הדלת.
מה יעזור לי:
שתגידו לי בשקט שראיתם, ושזה בסדר.
ואחר כך ננקה ביחד.

אל תשאלו אותי כל רגע
״אורי, צריך פיפי?״ שוב ושוב,
ואני דווקא מחזיק חזק יותר.
מה יעזור לי:
שאגיד לכם בעצמי כשאני מרגיש,
ואחרי האוכל נשב ביחד על הסיר.

השירותים בגן מפחידים
הם גדולים, והדלת נסגרת חזק.
אני מעדיף לא להיכנס.
מה יעזור לי:
שתבואו איתי לשירותים של הגן
לפני שהיום מתחיל, ושיהיה לי סיר בחדר.

כל ניסיון נחשב
גם כשאני יושב ולא יוצא כלום,
תגידו לי ״כל הכבוד שניסית״.
מדבקה אחת על הלוח,
וזה מחזיר לי את פעם.

זה לא נשאר לנצח
אמא ואבא, אני לא מפספס כדי להרגיז.
הרבה ילדים חוזרים לפספס לכמה ימים,
או כמה שבועות, ואז זה עובר.
תהיו איתי עד אז, ונחזור לפעם.

אפשר גם לעזור להם
עם הפספוסים אחרי הגמילה
בעזרת ספר מותאם אישית.

sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. ... Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... Ask them why this might be ... Listen to their response ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Check with the pediatrician first; a change like a new child-care routine is a common cause; ask the child why and listen; hugs, praise and stickers on a chart; it usually does not last very long, a few days or weeks in many cases. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up ... constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins
sources.supports: From about age 3 children can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticize or punish; say you know, that it is okay and that next time will go better; ask for help cleaning up; constant asking can make a child hold back until it is too late; avoid returning to diapers, use training pants, the potty in the child's room, going with the child to the preschool bathroom. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, date reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals ... Offer your child small rewards, such as stickers or time reading, every time your child goes in the potty. ... Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. ... It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. Reassure your child that he or she is well on the way to using the potty like a big kid.
sources.supports: Sit on the potty 15 to 30 minutes after meals, small rewards like stickers or reading time, praise every attempt even if nothing happens, no punishment and no disappointed face, say it was an accident and reassure the child. A Nemours page for parents.

sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. ... Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... Ask them why this might be ... Listen to their response ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Check with the pediatrician first; a change like a new child-care routine is a common cause; ask the child why and listen; hugs, praise and stickers on a chart; it usually does not last very long, a few days or weeks in many cases. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up ... constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins
sources.supports: From about age 3 children can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticize or punish; say you know, that it is okay and that next time will go better; ask for help cleaning up; constant asking can make a child hold back until it is too late; avoid returning to diapers, use training pants, the potty in the child's room, going with the child to the preschool bathroom. An American Academy of Pediatrics family page.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, date reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Have your child sit on the potty within 15 to 30 minutes after meals ... Offer your child small rewards, such as stickers or time reading, every time your child goes in the potty. ... Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. ... It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. Reassure your child that he or she is well on the way to using the potty like a big kid.
sources.supports: Sit on the potty 15 to 30 minutes after meals, small rewards like stickers or reading time, praise every attempt even if nothing happens, no punishment and no disappointed face, say it was an accident and reassure the child. A Nemours page for parents.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.quote: Talk about others' feelings. ... Suggest how children can show empathy. For example, “Let's get Jason some ice for his boo-boo.” ... Read stories about feelings. ... Be a role model. When you have strong, respectful relationships and interact with others in a kind and caring way, your child learns from your example.
sources.supports: Talk about others' feelings, suggest how a child can show empathy with a short sentence, read stories about feelings and be a role model. The page is about infants and toddlers; used as general advice for older children and as support for reading stories about feelings.

זה משפט שאפשר להגיד גם אני.

אני הולך אליו
צעד אחד.
ועוד צעד.
אני יושב לידו על הרצפה.
ואומר את המשפט.
בקול קטן.

הוא מסתכל עליי
הוא מנגב את העיניים
ואומר ״כואב לי״.
ואני אומר ״נלך ביחד לגננת״.
הבכי נהיה קטן יותר.

תתרגלו איתי עוד משפטים
מה יעזור לי:
שתתרגלו איתי משפט, כמו בבית,
ותספרו לי מה אתם עושים כשמישהו עצוב.
ובבוקר:
שתגידו לי ״ראינו שעזרת, גיא״.

עוד לא תמיד אצליח
אמא ואבא, לפעמים אני עדיין קופא.
זה בסדר, ואני לומד.
כשאתם מדברים על זה בבית,
קל לי יותר לזוז.

אפשר גם לעזור להם
עם נתינה לאחרים
בעזרת ספר מותאם אישית.
תכתבו "עזרה"
ואשלח לכם קישור להכנת הספר 📖

sources.title: How to Be a Kindness Role Model for Your Kids
sources.publisher: Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley (Dale V. Atkins and Amanda R. Salzhauer, 13 Nov 2018)
sources.quote: We can observe and notice opportunities for kindness all around us, offer small acts of kindness to others, and talk to our children about what we are doing and why. ... When you're watching a movie or TV show with your child, talk about how one of the characters might be feeling and how you would feel in that situation. ... highlight ways in which they were showing empathy. ... Talking to our kids about why we give and how it impacts us and others is vital ... if you or your child loves to draw, turn some of the drawings into cards for people who are in the hospital.
sources.supports: Observe opportunities for kindness, offer small acts of kindness and talk to children about what we are doing and why; talk about how a story character feels; highlight the ways a child showed empathy; talk about why we give; turn drawings into cards for people in the hospital. A Greater Good Science Center (UC Berkeley) article for parents.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.quote: Talk about others' feelings. ... Suggest how children can show empathy. For example, “Let's get Jason some ice for his boo-boo.” ... Read stories about feelings. ... Be a role model. When you have strong, respectful relationships and interact with others in a kind and caring way, your child learns from your example.
sources.supports: Talk about others' feelings, suggest how a child can show empathy with a short sentence, read stories about feelings and be a role model. The page is about infants and toddlers; used as general advice for older children and as support for reading stories about feelings.
